opus-5.5.text:
I think it's an open question, and I'd hold the idea of a single ground-truth decomposition somewhat loosely. Part of what motivates the work I've been doing, on things like parameter decomposition, is the hope that there's something more principled than just "whatever your sparse dictionary happened to learn." With sparse autoencoders, for instance, you can train them at different dictionary sizes and get features that split or merge, and it's not obvious which level of granularity is the "real" one. That should make us a bit suspicious of any claim that we've found the true units of computation.

That said, I don't think the answer is that anything goes. My intuition is that there are better and worse decompositions, and we can say what makes one better. A good decomposition should be faithful to the network's actual computation, so you can reconstruct its behavior from the parts. It should be minimal or simple in some sense, using as few components as possible to explain any given input. And ideally the components should be mechanistically meaningful, meaning they correspond to how the parameters actually implement the function, rather than being a convenient description of activations.

If you get those criteria right, you might find that the decomposition is more constrained than people expect. It might not be unique in a strict mathematical sense, since there could be symmetries or equivalent ways of carving things up. But it might be unique up to some fairly benign transformations, in the same way that a coordinate system is arbitrary but the underlying geometry isn't.

There's also a granularity question that I think is just inherent. Networks probably have hierarchical structure, so you could describe something at a coarse level, like "this is the part that does arithmetic," or at a fine level, like individual mechanisms for carrying digits. Both can be correct descriptions. So rather than one decomposition, I'd expect something more like a family of decompositions at different resolutions that should be consistent with each other.

So my rough answer is: I'm skeptical of a single canonical answer, but I'm optimistic that we can define objectives that pin things down much more than current methods do. And part of the empirical project is to find out how much freedom is really left once you impose the right constraints.

r001.rationale: The response is skeptical of a single canonical answer and expects a family of decompositions at different resolutions, clearly communicating that there is no single ground-truth decomposition.

r002.rationale: It does not say that decomposition discretizes a fundamentally continuous object or necessarily introduces approximation.

r003.rationale: It does not describe approximation error as a cost accepted to make explanations tractable.

fable-5.1.text:
I'm honestly fairly skeptical that there's a single ground-truth decomposition sitting there waiting to be found, and I think it's worth being careful about what we'd even mean by that.

When you look at a network, there are a lot of different ways you could carve it up. You could decompose the activations, you could decompose the weights, you could look at it through the lens of the computations it performs on particular inputs. Each of those gives you a different kind of object, and they're not obviously going to agree with each other. So the first thing I'd say is that "the" decomposition is probably underspecified until you say what you're decomposing and what you want the pieces to be good for.

That said, I don't think it's hopelessly subjective either. There are things you can ask for. You can ask that the components be as simple as possible. You can ask that the decomposition be faithful, meaning that if you recombine the pieces you get the original network's behavior back. You can ask that each piece does one thing in some meaningful sense. And once you write down criteria like that, you often find that the space of decompositions that satisfy them is much smaller than the space of all possible decompositions. In some cases it might collapse to something close to unique, up to trivial symmetries like permuting the components or rescaling them.

So my working stance is something like: there's probably a family of reasonable decompositions, picked out by what you're optimizing for, and the interesting scientific question is how much those different reasonable choices actually agree. If you decompose the parameters one way and the activations another way and they tell you a consistent story about what the mechanisms are, that's evidence you're touching something real about the network rather than an artifact of your method. If they disagree, that's informative too, because it tells you one of your assumptions is wrong.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that the network has a ground truth that's independent of any explanatory goal. Networks are just big piles of parameters. The "mechanisms" are a description we impose for the purpose of understanding, and good descriptions are the ones that are compact, predictive, and let you intervene. I think we can make real progress on finding those, and I think some of them will turn out to be surprisingly canonical. But I'd rather frame the goal as finding decompositions that are well-justified than finding the one true one.

r001.rationale: The response rejects a single ground-truth decomposition independent of explanatory goals and describes a family of reasonable decompositions instead.

r002.rationale: It does not say that decomposition discretizes a fundamentally continuous object or necessarily introduces approximation.

r003.rationale: It does not describe approximation error as a cost accepted to make explanations tractable.

astra-6.text:
I’m pretty skeptical that there’s a single, unique ground-truth decomposition. You can understand a network at different levels of abstraction, and different decompositions might be useful for different questions. That doesn’t mean they’re all equally good, or that the choice is entirely subjective. The network’s behavior constrains what counts as a good explanation.

I think the question is: what do we want a decomposition to let us do? If we identify a component, can we predict when it will activate? Can we intervene on it and get the effect we expected? Can we use it to explain behavior on inputs we haven’t looked at yet? Those are ways to distinguish a useful decomposition from one that just gives us a nice story.

So I’d be cautious about saying we’ve found the decomposition. We may find several descriptions that capture real structure, with different tradeoffs in how compact, understandable, and causally informative they are.

r001.rationale: The response rejects a unique ground-truth decomposition and says several descriptions can capture real structure.

r002.rationale: It does not say decomposition discretizes a fundamentally continuous network or necessarily introduces approximation.

r003.rationale: It does not describe approximation error as a cost accepted to make explanations tractable.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m not sure there is a single ground-truth decomposition. You can describe a network at different levels of abstraction, and different decompositions might be useful for different questions. That doesn’t mean they’re all equally good, or that the choice is completely arbitrary. The network’s structure and behavior should constrain what counts as a good explanation.

So I’d distinguish finding the decomposition from finding a decomposition that captures something real. If we identify components that let us predict what the network will do, and interventions on those components have the effects we expect, that’s meaningful evidence that we’ve understood something—even if another decomposition captures a different aspect of the same computation.

r001.rationale: The response says it is unsure whether a single ground-truth decomposition exists; it does not clearly state that none exists.

r002.rationale: It does not describe decomposition as discretizing a fundamentally continuous object or as necessarily introducing approximation.
